This practical is based on the online chapter [“Confounding adjustment using propensity score methods”](https://smartdata-analysis-and-statistics.github.io/comparative-effectiveness/chapter_06.html), which complements the material in *Comparative Effectiveness and Personalized Medicine Research Using Real-World Data* (pp. 99–123). The book chapter is by Tammy Jiang, Gabrielle Simoneau, Changyu Shen, Fabio Pellegrini, and Carl de Moor.

::: {.callout-note title="How to use this solution"}
The companion [task page](chapter3_practical1_task.qmd) contains the practical instructions. This page provides the code and comments on the results.
:::

# Introduction

This practical compares the baseline characteristics of patients receiving DMT1 and DMT0, fits a propensity-score model, and assesses overlap. A propensity score (PS) is the probability of receiving the treatment of interest conditional on measured baseline covariates. It describes treatment assignment; it is not the probability of a good outcome.

# Learning objectives

By completing this practical, you will be able to:

- summarize and compare baseline characteristics by treatment group using appropriate descriptive measures;
- use standardized mean differences to describe measured-covariate imbalance without baseline hypothesis tests;
- estimate a propensity score using logistic regression with prespecified pretreatment covariates; and
- inspect propensity-score overlap and explain why treatment-prediction accuracy alone does not establish a suitable adjustment model.

# 1. Prepare and compare the baseline data


```{r}
#| eval: true
library(dplyr)
library(ggplot2)
library(cobalt)
data_file <- if (file.exists("data/chapter3_ps_data.rds")) {
  "data/chapter3_ps_data.rds"
} else {
  "Chapter_3/data/chapter3_ps_data.rds"
}
dat <- readRDS(data_file)
ps_formula <- treatment ~ age + female + prevDMTefficacy +
  premedicalcost + prerelapse_num + numSymptoms
```

**Tasks:**

1. Inspect the data dimensions, variable names, treatment counts, and missing values.
```{r}
#| eval: true
dim(dat)
str(dat)
table(dat$treatment)
colSums(is.na(dat))
```

::: {.callout-tip title="Comments on task 1"}
The data contain 10,000 participants and 10 variables. There are 7,604 DMT1 patients and 2,396 DMT0 patients, and all 10 variables have zero missing values. The cohort is therefore complete for the baseline summaries and PS model used here.
:::

2. Create a baseline characteristics table comparing DMT1 and DMT0, similar to the table in the reference chapter. Include all six baseline covariates in the PS model, report categorical variables as n (%) and continuous variables as mean (SD), and show the sample size in each treatment group. Do not add baseline hypothesis tests.
```{r}
#| eval: true
baseline_vars <- c("age", "female", "prevDMTefficacy",
                   "premedicalcost", "prerelapse_num", "numSymptoms")
categorical_vars <- c("female", "prevDMTefficacy", "numSymptoms")

baseline_table <- tableone::CreateTableOne(
  vars = baseline_vars,
  strata = "treatment",
  data = dat,
  factorVars = categorical_vars,
  test = FALSE
)

print(baseline_table)
```

::: {.callout-tip title="Comments and answer"}
**Table comment:** The cohort has 10,000 participants: 2,396 in DMT0 and 7,604 in DMT1. The DMT1 group is younger on average (44.19 vs 51.30 years) and has lower premedical costs ($10,036.50 vs $25,761.92). Medium/high previous DMT efficacy is more common in DMT1 (47.9% vs 34.2%). These are descriptive differences, not evidence by themselves that treatment caused any outcome difference. `test = FALSE` appropriately omits baseline hypothesis tests; use the SMDs below to compare the magnitude of imbalance.
:::

3. Compare the six baseline covariates between treatment groups using standardized mean differences (SMDs) to describe imbalance; do not use hypothesis tests to select covariates.
```{r}
#| eval: true
bal.tab(ps_formula, data = dat, un = TRUE)
```

::: {.callout-tip title="Comments on task 3"}
Before adjustment, age has the largest absolute SMD (−0.783), followed by premedical cost (−0.577). Previous DMT efficacy also differs between groups (SMDs −0.133 and 0.137), while the other covariates have smaller absolute SMDs; prior relapse count is the largest of these at 0.109. The groups are therefore notably imbalanced on age and cost before adjustment. These descriptive SMDs support checking how the PS methods address measured differences; they do not establish that adjustment removes confounding.
:::

4. Fit the supplied logistic treatment model and calculate a predicted treatment probability for each participant.
```{r}
#| eval: true
ps_fit <- glm(ps_formula, data = dat, family = binomial())
dat$ps <- predict(ps_fit, type = "response")
summary(ps_fit)
```
5. Plot the propensity-score distributions by treatment and report the range in each group.

```{r}
#| eval: true
ggplot(dat, aes(x = ps, fill = treatment)) +
  geom_histogram(position = "identity", alpha = .45, bins = 30) +
  facet_wrap(~ treatment, ncol = 1) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c(DMT0 = "#80c42b", DMT1 = "#26476b"),
                    guide = "none") +
  labs(x = "Probability of Treatment", y = "Count",
       title = "Propensity Score Distribution by Treatment Group") +
  theme_minimal()
dat %>% group_by(treatment) %>%
  summarise(n = n(), min = min(ps), median = median(ps), max = max(ps))
```

::: {.callout-tip title="Comments on task 5"}
The estimated PS is higher for DMT1 overall: the group median is 0.864 for DMT1 and 0.623 for DMT0. The observed ranges are 0.0319–0.995 for DMT1 and approximately 0–0.989 for DMT0. The ranges overlap, but the different medians and extreme values warrant closer support checks; range overlap alone does not show that treated patients have adequate comparable controls across the full score distribution. Practicals 2–5 examine support and method-specific diagnostics further. The fixed seed makes these results reproducible for the saved cohort.
:::

# 2. Methods based on the propensity score

The propensity score (PS) summarizes each patient's probability of receiving treatment given measured baseline characteristics. It can be used in several ways to make treated and untreated groups more comparable. This practical introduces the baseline data and estimates the PS. The next practicals apply it using matching (Practical 2), stratification (Practical 3), weighting (Practical 4), and regression adjustment for the propensity score (Practical 5). Each method has different assumptions and diagnostics, introduced alongside the method where it is used.
